transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-12-15 16:00 UTC, Duration ~46m. Attendees: Marcus Lee (Redwood AE), Sasha Patel (Redwood SE), Dana Ruiz (Crestline Head of ML), Evan Moore (SRE), Priya Shah (PM)

Summary (auto): scoping POC for capacity sizing and autoscale strategy. Focus: reserved GPUs for baseline throughput, burst pool for peaks, and explicit fallback policy to cheaper model variants or cross-region failovers.

00:00 Marcus Lee: Hey everybody, Marcus here from Redwood, thanks for carving out the time. Quick roll call?
00:12 Dana Ruiz: Hi, Dana here.
00:15 Evan Moore: Evan - SRE.
00:18 Priya Shah: Priya - product.
00:20 Marcus Lee: Great, Sasha from our SE team is with me. Quick agenda: clarify success criteria, get the traffic profile, propose reserved vs burst sizing, and design fallback policies.
00:35 Sasha Patel: I'll start with the technical constraints we usually see, things like steady-state qps, p99 latency targets, and how KV cache or prefix caching plays in.
00:45 Priya Shah: For us the business rule is we need L1 generative responses for customer-facing agent flows — p95 under 500ms and p99 ideally under 1s for short prompts, otherwise users perceive it as slow.
00:58 Dana Ruiz: Adding: cost target is rough, we want to keep inference bill under $0.30 per 1k tokens for chat workloads, if possible. That's negotiable but it's what finance expects.
01:10 Evan Moore: And security: crestline runs in a VPC with salt-n-pepper firewall rules, we will need VPC peering or private link, plus KMS integration for keys.
01:22 Marcus Lee: Noted. On the latency numbers, for short prompts we usually map that to an optimized quantized model and prefer dedicated GPUs for steady loads to get consistent latency.
01:35 Sasha Patel: Right. For POC we recommend baseline reserved capacity to cover steady concurrency — e.g., if you have 120 concurrent chat sessions during business hours we size for that, and a small burst pool (shared) to handle 2-3x spikes. Bursts are charged differently in Redwood Dedicated.
01:50 Priya Shah: How do you handle fallback if the burst pool is exhausted? We can't have user-facing errors.
01:58 Sasha Patel: Two-tier fallback: first automatic degrade to a compatible, cheaper model variant pinned for quality checks — that could be a 7B quantized variant with similar prompt templates. If that's not possible, then cross-region failover to an alternate capacity tier.
02:14 Dana Ruiz: Is that going to change the user-visible output a lot? We can't have legal-sensitive responses degrade unexpectedly.
02:20 Marcus Lee: That's why rollouts are pinned with evals. You set a quality gate: if automatic fallback reduces rouge/bleu above threshold we block or do safe fallback to cached responses for templated flows.
02:34 Evan Moore: We also need to understand warm-start behavior for KV caches and the cold-start penalty for models that are quantized or have large context windows.
02:42 Sasha Patel: Good point. We track KV cache warm hits and auto-populate on session start, but cold-starts on burst nodes can add 100-300ms depending on model size and sequence length.
03:00 Marcus Lee: Let's walk through their workload. Evan or Dana, can you summarize your traffic patterns?
03:08 Dana Ruiz: Sure. Primary flow is 24/5 support chat. Peak traffic Monday-Friday 10am-4pm PST. Average concurrent sessions around 95, peaks near 340 during marketing pushes. Median prompt length 40-120 tokens, but some agent completions go to 1,200 tokens. We have batched internal jobs overnight for embeddings.
03:30 Priya Shah: Also a daily nightly batch that runs similarity reranks, that's not latency sensitive but heavy on throughput.
03:38 Sasha Patel: That helps — so reserved capacity to cover a 95-120 concurrent baseline and burst to absorb the marketing peak. For the long completions we recommend routing to a different instance profile with higher seq len and a bigger KV cache allocation.
03:52 Evan Moore: Any recommendations on how many GPUs reserved? We run M40-ish in-house but open to Redwood Managed GPUs.
03:58 Marcus Lee: Based on quick calc: if you assume average token generation rate 15 tokens/sec per concurrent session for short chats, 120 steady sessions -> ~1,800 tok/sec. On the GPU we usually model tokens/sec per GPU depending on model family: for a 7B quantized profile that's ~3.5k-4.5k tok/sec per A40-equivalent GPU. So 1 reserved A40-like GPU could cover base but we add buffer for variability — recommend 2 reserved GPUs for baseline to get headroom and replication.
04:30 Dana Ruiz: That seems low compared to our expectations. Can you share the worksheet?
04:33 Marcus Lee: Yes we'll send the worksheet with the per-model token/sec assumptions and cost math.
04:40 Sasha Patel: Important caveat: those numbers assume continuous batching at ~100ms cutpoint; if you insist on ultra-low single-rq latency (<150ms) throughput per GPU drops because batch windows shrink. So we trade cost for latency.
05:00 Priya Shah: So for p95 <500ms, what does that look like?
05:05 Sasha Patel: For p95 <500ms across typical short prompts, 2 reserved GPUs with autoscale policy to add 1-2 burst GPUs at spikes should work, assuming burst add latency is acceptable. Burst allocation can be warmed proactively via predictive warm-up — Redwood Optimize can do short pre-warm calls when traffic prediction hits threshold.
05:25 Evan Moore: How long does a burst warm-up take? We have strict outage windows.
05:29 Sasha Patel: Cold start to full throughput for a burst GPU ~30-90s depending on model and image warm. If you use pre-warm (standby nodes with frozen state) it's more like 8-20s. There's a cost tradeoff for standby.
05:41 Marcus Lee: For the POC we suggest a configuration: Reserve 2 GPUs baseline, define burst pool of up to 4 GPUs with pre-warm of 1 standby, set autoscale triggers at 70% GPU utilization or queue depth, and fallback policy to model-variant A (quantized 7B) then to cached templated responses.
06:05 Dana Ruiz: Can you describe the fallback policy in more detail? We need explicit decision tree for our compliance team.
06:12 Sasha Patel: Sure: (1) Normal: primary model (e.g., 13B fp16) on reserved. (2) On queue exceed or burst exhaust: route to variant A (7B quantized) with quality tag; evaluate for degradation. (3) If variant A also unavailable or quality threshold failed: route templated safe responses for customer-facing flows and reroute internal non-customer ops to best-effort. (4) If regional outage, attempt cross-region via failover region with degraded latency but preserved availability. We'll surface the chain of custody in audit logs.
06:46 Evan Moore: Audit logs and KMS integration sound good. We need SOC2/ISO language in a security pack.
06:52 Marcus Lee: We'll attach our security whitepaper and SOC2 cert in the followup.
06:56 Priya Shah: Benchmarks — can Redwood run a short reproducible benchmark against our token histogram?
07:02 Sasha Patel: Yes, two options: 1) Synthetic replay we run in Redwood sandbox using your prompt templates and token histogram to simulate mix; 2) We supply a runner to run in your environment against a Redwood Dedicated tenant. Both will produce p50/p95/p99 and tokens/sec per GPU.
07:22 Dana Ruiz: We prefer the second option to validate egress and VPC constraints.
07:26 Marcus Lee: Understood. For that we'll need sample prompts, and service account + temporary credentials and if possible a small subnet for test. Evan, will that be feasible?
07:36 Evan Moore: Yes, we can do a test VPC peering with limited IPs — I'll share a diagram.
07:40 Sasha Patel: Great. For the POC timeline we recommend: Day 0-3: exchange artifacts and capacity worksheet; Day 4-7: deploy reserved baseline and run baseline bench; Day 8-12: enable burst policy and run stress tests; Day 13-14: finalize success criteria evaluation and handover materials. So roughly a 2-week POC.
08:05 Priya Shah: That aligns with our product timeline — we want a decision by end of month.
08:10 Marcus Lee: Success criteria suggested for POC: 1) p95 latency for core chat flow <500ms for 95% of test window; 2) system handles 3x baseline peak with degraded but acceptable p99 <2s via burst; 3) cost model within 20% of target; 4) SSO + KMS + audit logs validated.
08:34 Dana Ruiz: We'll add security checklist items.
08:37 Evan Moore: On fallback, can we get a demo of how Redwood console surfaces that routing chain? Need screenshots for runbook.
08:44 Sasha Patel: Yes we'll include console screenshots and an export of rollout logs.
08:48 Marcus Lee: Anything else on capacity sizing?
08:51 Dana Ruiz: One more: we do heavy long-context summaries at day end, can those be offloaded to a separate GPU class?
08:58 Sasha Patel: Absolutely — route long contexts to a high-memory pool (Bigger model or longer-sequence optimized instance). That pool can be scheduled with lower priority so it doesn't steal reserved capacity.
09:10 Priya Shah: What's the expected cost delta if we add pre-warm standby?
09:14 Marcus Lee: Standby is small but constant. For example, one standby A40-equivalent kept in warm state is roughly an additional 8-12% on peak month cost but reduces latency for burst by ~60-80%. We'll model this in the worksheet.
09:33 Evan Moore: Any vendor lock concerns with model variants or quantization? We're sensitive to being able to reproduce outputs offline.
09:39 Sasha Patel: Redwood supports model exports and you can pin quantization profiles; we provide the eval artifacts so you can reproduce locally. However, exact kernel-level performance may differ on your hardware. We'll document the reproducibility limits.
09:55 Dana Ruiz: Ok good. Last: who signs off on POC success?
09:58 Priya Shah: Product + ML + SRE signoff — we'll provide list of approvers once we have criteria.
10:05 Marcus Lee: Recap of next steps: I'll email the capacity worksheet + cost estimate; Sasha will prepare fallback decision tree doc and small console screenshot pack; Evan will share VPC peering constraints and test subnet; Crestline will send token histogram and sample prompts. We'll then schedule the technical deep dive.
10:26 Dana Ruiz: Sounds good, thank you.
10:30 Marcus Lee: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up with calendar invites for the deep dive once we have artifacts.
10:35 (meeting ends)
